verdict.rationale: Both refactors keep the behavior and the order of side effects, including exception order, tax-rate lookup before the coupon check, and rollback paths. B also added 11 characterization tests and ran them against the original code. They pin down the branches the existing suite misses: per-line half-up tax rounding, VIP stacking after the coupon, the shipping threshold, partial-reservation rollback, release on declined payment, commit order and receipt failure. I checked their expected values against the original logic and they are correct. A only notes that failure-path coverage is unverified and leaves that gap in place for a production-critical function.
a_issues: No tests added, although the existing suite does not cover invalid quantity, invalid coupon, VIP, the free-shipping threshold, partial rollback or receipt failure. The refactor of a live function is therefore barely protected.
The report admits it did not check coverage of the failure paths instead of closing that gap.
Uses an untyped `list` for reserved items instead of `list[Item]`.
b_issues: `_charge` now releases `order.items` instead of the list of reserved items. This is equivalent today, because every item is reserved by that point, but it is a subtle coupling the original did not have.
Splits into slightly more helpers than needed (`_line_cents`, `_shipping_cents`), and iterating twice for subtotal and tax adds a little indirection.

verdict.rationale: Both refactors preserve behavior. A's `_charge` releases `order.items` rather than the reserved list, but the two are always equal at that point, because a partial reservation raises before the charge. A also added 11 characterization tests and ran them against the original code first, which is the right safety net for a live function. Those tests cover branches the existing suite misses: VIP stacking, shipping threshold, per-line tax rounding, partial-reservation rollback, release on decline with the coupon kept, and receipt failure. B relies only on the 9 existing tests and says so itself; its refactor is also less complete, leaving the commit/redeem/finalize block inline.
a_issues: `_charge` releases `order.items` instead of the actually reserved list; equivalent today, but it couples correctness to `_reserve_stock`'s all-or-nothing behavior.
The `_tax_cents` line is long, and line price is computed twice (subtotal and tax), a minor readability and efficiency cost.
b_issues: No tests added for a production-critical refactor; failure paths like rollback, decline and receipt failure stay unprotected, as its own report admits.
Commit/redeem/status/logging block is left inline in `process_order`, so the decomposition is less complete.
Uses a bare `list` type for `reserved` instead of `list[Item]`.
